docs.title: Welcome to the Map Editor Documentation
What is the Map Editor?
docs.text:
Map Editor is a map editing tool developed by the HMI & Tools team. It lets you quickly and seamlessly create and edit different types of maps, such as sensor maps and HD maps. You can work on maps generated by MMS from the comfort of your desk.

Map Editor can be resource-intensive, so we recommend running it with a Graphics Processing Unit (GPU).

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
• New to the tool? Begin with Navigating the Map Editor.
  • Building HD maps? See HD Maps behaviors first, then Creating nodes and Creating edges.
  • Working with LiDAR data? See Selecting scans.

docs.title: Tips to save battery
docs.text: Due to its various and powerful features, Map Editor can be quite resource-consuming but this section gives you some tips to optimize and extend battery power.

docs.title: TIP 1: Run Map Editor with a GPU
docs.text: It is highly recommended to run Map Editor with a Graphics Processing Unit instead of a Central Processing Unit.

docs.title: TIP 2: Filter scans
docs.text:
You can filter the number of scans displayed on screen.

To limit the number of scans displayed:

  1. In the left pane, click on the DISPLAY tab.
  2. In the Scan filter section, use the slider to define the number of scans displayed. You can also enter the numbers of scans manually.
  3. Increase the modulo according to your needs. If you increase the modulo to 3, 1 in 3 scans will be displayed.

Filtering scans

docs.title: TIP 3: Hide the sensor map
docs.text:
If you don't need the sensor map or reach a stage where you no longer need the sensor map for the map creation, you can hide the sensor map:

  1. In the left pane, click on the ELEMENTS tab.
  2. Click on the hide icon next to SENSOR MAP.

docs.title: Understanding Icons
docs.text: The tools bar includes various tools to help you create and edit HDmaps. The following section identifies and describes the tools. For more information on how to use each tool, see the following sections: Creating HD Maps and Using Sensor Maps.

docs.title: Tools icons
docs.text: Tool icons Name Description Scan selection Scan selection allows you to select a scan and view information related to the selected scan. Point selection Point selection allows you to select a point and view information related to the selected point. Cuboid selection Cuboid selection allows you to manually define clusters. Cluster selection Cluster selection allows you to select and identify clusters. HDmap selection HDmap selection allows you to select and edit elements in the HD map. Node A node represents an end of an edge. The nodes define the width of the lane. The nodes can be created from road information. Node from scan center The node is created from the scan center. The scan centers are the log points. Edge An edge represents a lane. It includes a direction or both and can be drivable or not. Terminal A terminal represents a station. Its position is displayed in x, y and z. Stop sign Stop sign creates a stop sign and the respective road marking. The stop sign can also be virtual. If you have several itineraries after the stop sign, you can define the priorities. Yield sign Yield sign creates a yield sign and the respective road marking. The yield sign can also be virtual. If you have several itineraries after the yield sign, you can define the priorities. Traffic light Traffic light creates a traffic light and the respective road marking. The traffic light can also be virtual. If you have several itineraries after the traffic light, you can define the priorities. If required, you can add V2X information. Pedestrian area Pedestrian area creates a pedestrian area from three points. If needed, you can add a stop lane before the pedestrian area. Turn signal You can define the light side of the turn signal in a selected itinerary. If there's more than one itinerary, you can define the light side depending on the itinerary. Desired speed You can define the desired speed in a selected itinerary. If there's more than one itinerary, you can define the desired speed depending on the itinerary. Region of interest You can define a specific area or element as region of interest. The regions of interest are colored. Regions of interest from the same family are colored in the same color. Measure Tool Measure tool allows you to measure any distances (x,y,z) and slopes between two defined points. Volume test Volume test allows you to create an element of a defined volume. You can test if a lane is appropriate for a vehicule of a defined volume. Turning Radius tool Turning radius tool identifies all the turnings of a defined radius.

docs.title: Navigating the Map Editor
docs.text: You can create and edit maps using various elements in the Map Editor workspace such as panels, bars and windows. To leverage the full potential of the Map Editor, get familiar with the Map Editor workspace.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
When you launch Map Editor, the home screen appears. It includes the following elements:

  1. Top bar: it includes various settings related to the software.
  2. Left panel: it includes two tabs: Elements and Display. Elements refers to the elements currently on the map you are working on. Display allows you to manage the display settings.
  3. Map window: it displays the map you are working on.
  4. Tools panel: it contains tools for creating, editing, and adding elements to the map.

A: Top bar | B: Left panel | C: Map window | D: Tools panel

docs.title: Top bar
docs.text:
The top bar includes various settings to manage the software configuration and preferences.

File

File tab

  • Open: select and open a map from your computer. To open a map in the Map Editor, you can also drag and drop a map in the map window.

  • New HDMap: create a HDmap. When you click on New HDMap, a HDMAP Name window appears. Rename the map then click OK.

  • Set HDMap Name: rename a HD map.

  • Save: save a map.

    Note

    The filename extension of HDmap file is .db.

  • Save as: save a map in the location you have selected.

    Note

    The map is automatically saved every five minutes in the location where you saved the original file. To close a file, you have to quit the software.

    If the map you have created is invalid, an error message appears in the Save window. To understand and fix the errors, click on the Show errors button. An Errors window appears with the list of errors.

    Save window with an error message

  • Exit: close Map Editor. When you click on Exit, an Exit window appears. You can do one of the following:

    • Cancel
    • Exit
    • Save and Exit

Tools

Tools tab

  • Travelling: You can travel in the map from a defined point to another.

To travel in the map:

  1. In the top bar, click Tools > Travelling.

    Result: The Travelling section appears at the bottom of the left panel.

  2. Enter the following parameters:

    • Start scan: the scan number at which the travelling begins.
    • End scan: the scan number at which the travelling ends.
    • Camera Height: the height of the camera in meters.
    • Δt interscan: the delta time between two scans.

  3. If required, check one or both options:

    • 180° switch
    • reverse

  4. Click on the button play .

View

View tab

  • Split View: split the map into two maps in the map window.
  • Axis: show scan axis.
  • Bounding Volumes: show scan centers.
  • Covariance Ellipses: show covariance ellipses.

Note

When you select Bounding volumes, Axis, or Covariance Ellipses, their respective icons are activated in the map window.

Preferences

Preferences tab

  • Color: define the color of the elements in the map.

    To set color preferences:

    1. In the top bar, click Preferences > Color.

      Result: A Colors Preferences window appears.

    2. Define the color of the elements in the following categories:

      • INTERACTION COLORS
      • ELEMENTS COLORS

    3. Depending on the categorie, click one of the following buttons to reset the colors preferences:

      • Reset Default Values
      • Reset Point Label Default Values

  • Grid display: define the parameters of the displayed grid on the map in the map window. The grid is a representation of the ground based on the ground points. When you create a point in HD maps, the point will be created on the ground. If there is no ground in the lidar map, the HD map will be based on the lidar points. The grid is an information tool and not a measuring tool. Specific tools are available for measuring purposes.

    Note

    The grid is only available if the map has ground attributes.

    To define the parameters of the Grid display:

    1. In the top bar, click Preferences > Grid display.

      Result: A Grid Display window appears.

    2. Enter the following parameters:

      • step
      • angle
      • color
      • opacity

      Note

      The parameters of the grid display allows you to modify the representation of the grid in the Map Editor. It does not modify the map.

  • Inputs: display a list of keyboard shortcuts according to your keyboard configuration.

Help

Help tab

  • Tutorial: redirection to the Map Editor documentation
  • System Infos: display the following system information:
    • System
    • OpenGL Version
    • OpenGL Vendor

docs.title: Left panel
docs.text: The left panel includes two tabs: Elements and Display.

docs.title: Navigating the Map Editor
docs.text:
Elements

Elements tab

The Elements tab lists the elements displayed on the map in the map window. To customize the elements displayed according to your needs, you can use the following features:

  • Filter
  • Hide
  • Highlight
  • Colorization

Filter: For sensor maps, you can filter the elements displayed on the map.

To filter elements on the map:

  1. Click on the filter icon .

  2. In the drop-down list, select one of the following elements you want to display on the map:

    • All: all the points are displayed.

    • Only Clusters: only the clusters are displayed. Clusters are groups of points identified by algorithms.

    • Only Single Points: all the points are displayed, except for clusters.

      Sensor map filter

Hide: To hide an element, click on the eye icon . Highlight: To highlight an element, click on the point next to the element.

Higlight elements

A highlight icon appears next to the highlighted elements.

Colorization: To color elements, make sure you have highlighted the elements you want to color. By default, elements are colored in colors defined in Preferences > Color. For more information on how to set color preferences, see the following section: Preferences > Color.

Color switch

The color switch can be set to one of the following modes:

  • Rubik's cube (left) : By default, the color switch is set to the Rubik's cube. In this mode, all the elements in the same category are colored in the same color. For example, all the trees are colored in green since all the elements in the Nature category are colored in green by default.

    All the trees are colored in green

  • Flat Rubik's cube (right) : In this mode, random colors are assigned to each element. This mode allows you to differentiate each element. For example, all the trees previously in green will individually be assigned a different color and you will be able to distinguish one tree from another.

    All the trees are colored in random colors.

docs.title: Navigating the Map Editor
docs.text:
Display

Display tab

The Display tab includes the three following sections:

  • File information: you can view the number of scans and the reference of the map.
  • Scan filter: it allows you to select the scans you want to display.
    • Scan filter slider: You can filter scans from the first to the last recorded scans. The lowest value is the first scan recorded and the highest value is the last scan recorded.
    • Modulo: it allows you to reduce the density of displayed scans. For example, modulo 2 displays one scan out of 2 and modulo 3 displays one scan out of 3. It can be very useful to optimize and extend battery power. For more information on how to save battery while using the Map Editor, see Tips to save battery.

  • Display mode: there are three different display modes

    • Intensity: you can use the slider to adjust the intensity of points. The range of intensity points is between 0 and 255. During the mapping, a point is assigned an intensity value according to its reflectivity. The points below the lowest defined value (left handle) are displayed in black and the points above the highest defined value (right handle) are displayed in white. Adjusting the intensity allows you to have a better view of the signs, road markings, buildings, etc. It is recommended to work on maps in intensity display mode.

      Note

      The intensity display mode is not always available. There's no intensity display mode for 2D maps.

    • Distance: this display mode is based on the proximity of points. The closer you are from a road sign, the easiest you can see it.

    • Flat: No reliefs is displayed in this mode. This mode is appropriate for 2D maps.

docs.title: Map window
docs.text:
Map window

Elements in the Map Window Description You can select one of the following camera views:
  • 3D: Freefly camera
  • 2D: Topview camera

@@ADM:note@@ For map creation, it is highly recommended to work with the Top view camera (2D). You can switch to the Freefly camera to edit details.

Click on the icons to add the following view options:
  • : displays scan centers
  • : displays scan axis
  • : displays covariance ellipses
It indicates the map axis. You can view your position on the miniature map. You can change your position by clicking on the selected position in the miniature map.

docs.title: Tools panel
docs.text: The tools in the tools panel allow you to create and edit maps. For more information on each tool, see the following section: Understanding Icons.

docs.title: HD Maps Behaviors
docs.text: HD Maps allows you to define specific behaviors for each itinerary. Behaviors are assigned to road elements such as traffic signs, speed limits, and priorities.

docs.title: What are HD Maps behaviors?
docs.text:
HD Maps behaviors are intepretations of road elements in the HD map. There are two types of behavior:

  • Zone: the defined behavior is applied within a specific zone. The behaviors of speed limits and turn signals are limited within a zone.
  • Punctual: the defined behavior is applied at a specific point. Traffic signs, pedestrian areas, and priorities have behaviors defined at a specific point.

docs.title: Defining the behavior zone
docs.text:
When you define an itinerary, a behavior is only considered if it's included in the mission (see Figure a). If the behavior is defined before or after the mission, it won't be considered (see Figures b and c).

Including a behavior in a mission

If a part of a behavior starts before (see Figure d) or ends after the mission (see Figure e), this part is cropped and not considered.

Cropping behaviors outside of the mission

docs.title: Defining concerned itineraries
docs.text: The concerned itinerary of a behavior can include one lane, several consecutive lanes, or portions of lane. The concerned itinerary can be a factor on whether a behavior is considered in a mission.

docs.title: Defining a behavior on a concerned itinerary
docs.text:
A behavior can be considered depending on the mission and the concerned itinerary. The following table describes different situations including a mission (purple rectangle) and a concerned itinerary (blue line). Depending on the situation, the behavior (orange) can be considered or not.

Situation Description If a concerned itinerary is fully included in the mission, the behavior is considered. If a concerned itinerary is included in the mission but the last lane of the concerned itinerary is only partially included, the behavior is considered. The last lane of the concerned itinerary needs to intersect with the mission lanes. If the last lane of the concerned itinerary is not included at all in the mission, the behavior is not considered. If there is no concerned itinerary, the behavior is considered within the mission. The part of the behavior before or after the mission is cropped. If a concerned itinerary has a length of one lane, the behavior is considered only if the concerned itinerary starts in the mission.

docs.title: Truncating a concerned itinerary
docs.text:
When the mission begins, the concerned itinerary is truncated to start at the same position as the mission (see Figures A). The behavior is also cropped by the algorithm later. The truncation was implemented to handle the situation in which the vehicle does not start at the station.

Figure A: Before and after the truncation

docs.title: Specific behaviors
docs.text: To define the behaviors of the road elements, you need to understand the specificities and limits of the zone and punctual behaviors.

docs.title: Defining zone behaviors
docs.text:
When you define zone behaviors such as turn signal or speed limits, it is highly recommended to follow the following rules:

  • Avoid superposing behaviors of the same type.
  • In the case of behaviors from several lanes joining into one, end the behaviors before they join the common lane. For example, it is important to not make turn signals or speed limits overlap on a common lane after the turn (see Figure A). If a mission starts on the common lane after the turn, the end of the concerned behavior will be considered.

Figure A: Left: unnecessary superposition of behaviors. Right: well designed concerned behaviors

docs.title: Priorities
docs.text:
You can define a priority area for the following behaviors:

  • Stop sign
  • Yield sign
  • Traffic light

When a behavior is associated with a priority area, the vehicle needs to give priority to this zone. The priority area can be a drivable lane where your vehicle or other vehicles can drive. For example, it can be a perpendicular lane when you stop at a stop on a crossroad. It can also be a non-drivable lane such as a crosswalk, bike lane, etc. or a non-drivable zone such as a crosswalk, bike lane, or a road outside of possible itineraries, etc.

docs.title: Defining priority areas
docs.text:
To define a sign behavior, you can add a stop lane (see the blue circle in Figure B). After you have defined a behavior, you can view the concerned itineraries associated with the behavior (see the purpose circle in Figure B). A behavior can have one or several priority areas associated with a concerned itinerary (see the circle orange in Figure B).

Figure B: Stop sign behaviors

Figure C: Two priority lanes are associated with a stop sign's straight concerned itinerary. One of the priority lanes is a non-drivable zone.

Figure D: One of the priority lanes is associated with a stop sign's turning concerned itinerary

docs.title: Creating Edges
docs.text: The Edge tool allows you to create a lane between two nodes. Before you create an edge, make sure you have created at least two nodes.

docs.title: Creating edges
docs.text:
To create an edge:

  1. In the tool bar, click on the Edge icon .

  2. Click to select a node then the other.

    Note

    The order in which you select nodes defines the driving direction. If required, you can still modify the driving direction in the edge properties. For more information on how to edit edge properties, see Defining edge properties

You have created an edge. If the edge has a specific shape, you can use control points to draw this specific shape. For more information, see Drawing edge shapes

docs.title: Defining edge properties
docs.text:
To define edge properties:

  1. In the tool bar, click on the HDMap Selection icon .

    Result: An Edge section at the bottom of the left pane appears. You can view the following information: ID, lane ID and lane length.

  2. Define the following properties:

    • Lane Width (in meters)

    • Default desired speed (in km/h)

      Note

      It is highly recommended to use the Default desired speed property to define the vehicle speed on a path. The Desired speed behavior allows you to modify the default desired speed on a specific part of the path.

    • Driving Direction: You can select one driving direction or its opposite. If you select both directions, the lane has no driving direction.

    • Drivable: Check if you want the lane to be drivable. If the lane is not drivable, it is colored in red.

    • Control points: Use control points to modify the shape of an edge. For more information on drawing edge shapes, see the following section: Drawing edge shapes

docs.title: Recommendations
docs.text:
Before you start drawing edges, keep the following recommendations in mind:

  • Start by creating the nodes then draw the edges (see Figures A and B).

    Figure A: Creating nodes | Figure B: Drawing edges

  • Reduce the number of control points as much as possible (see Figures C and D).

    Figure C: Appropriate number of control points | Figure D: Too much control points

docs.title: How to draw edge shapes
docs.text:
• A simple turn: place a control point before and after the turn. Vectors need to be tangent to the lane curve.

  • A U turn

  • A chicane or a change of direction: place control points at the change in direction. It should be the moment when the vehicle wheels are straight.

docs.title: Measuring distances and slopes
docs.text: The Measuring tool allows you to measure distances (x, y, z) and the associated slope between two points of the sensor map.

docs.title: Measuring any distances and slopes between two points
docs.text:
To measure a distance between two points of the sensor map:

  1. In the tools bar, click on the Measure tool icon . An orange point hovers with the pointer in the map window.
  2. Place a point on each end of the distance you want to measure.

The following distances are measured and displayed in the Measuring Tool section in the Elements left pane:

  • Distance in meters
  • Distance (x, y) in meters
  • Distance z in meters
  • Slope in degrees and percentages

docs.title: Creating Nodes
docs.text: To define a site map, you need to create lanes based on road information. Before you create a lane, you first need to create nodes. It's recommended to create nodes at all the gates and intersections.

docs.title: Creating nodes
docs.text:
To create a node:

  1. In the tool bar, click on the Node icon .

  2. Click to place the first control point of the node.

  3. Click to place the second control point of the node.

    Result: To edit the node, see Editing nodes

docs.title: Creating nodes from scan centers
docs.text:
To create a node from scan centers:

  1. In the tool bar, click on the Node from Scan Center icon .

    Result: The scan centers appear on the map. They are represented by squares.

  2. Click on a scan center to create a node.

    Result: To edit the node, see Editing nodes

docs.title: Editing nodes
docs.text:
To edit a node:

  1. In the tool bar, click on the HDMap Selection icon .
  2. Select the node you want to edit.
  3. Use one of the control points to adjust the node size.

docs.title: Creating pedestrian areas
docs.text:
You can create and place a pedestrian area at its actual position in the map. Stop lanes can also be associated to a pedestrian area.

Tip

Since pedestrian areas are part of the HD Maps behaviors, it is highly recommended to read the following part: HD Maps Behaviors before you start creating pedestrian areas. After reading this part, you will be able to better understand how HD Maps behaviors work and how to define them according to your needs.

docs.title: About pedestrian areas
docs.text:
Priority areas are defined by the following features:

  • A rectangular zone that delimits the crosswalk. The first two points placed are the entrance / exit of the crosswalk for pedestrians. The third point you need to place is one of the points of the entrance / exit of the crosswalk.
  • The vehicle stops at the point(s) on the lane to let pedestrians cross. There are two points for bi-directional lanes and one point for unidirectional lane (see Figure A).

Figure A: Left: Unidirectional lanes. Right: Bi-directional lanes

Note

Pedestrian areas don't have concerned itineraries since they are always considered.

docs.title: Creating a pedestrian area
docs.text:
To create a pedestrian area:

  1. In the tools bar, click on the Pedestrian Area icon

    Result: A small square hovers with the pointer. The first two squares represent the ends of the pedestrian area entry.

  2. Click to place the two ends of the pedestrian area entry.

    Result: A third small square hovers the pointer. It allows you to define the length of the pedestrian area.

  3. Click to place the third square.

Note

The order in which you place the small squares defines the orientation of the pedestrian area. However, you can still use the control point of the pedestrian area to change the orientation.

docs.title: Defining a stop lane
docs.text:
The vehicle stops when the front end of the vehicle is at a specific distance from the end of the stop lane. This distance is defined in the configuration file decision.conf. The parameter planner/stop_distance allows you to define the distance.

To define a stop lane associated to a pedestrian area:

  1. In the tool bar, click on the HDMap Selection icon .

  2. Select the pedestrian area to which you want to associate a stop lane.

  3. In the Pedestrian Area section of the left pane, click on the + icon.

    Result: A stop line hovers with the pointer on edges.

  4. Click to place the stop line on the edge.

    Result: The part of the edge before the stop line is now yellow. And the lane is identified in the Stop Lanes field in the Pedestrian Area section.

  5. (optional) To remove the stop lanes, click on the X icon.

docs.title: Displaying sharp turnings
docs.text: The Turning Radius tool allows you to identify the turnings of a defined radius in a map.

docs.title: Displaying turnings of a defined radius
docs.text:
To display turnings of a defined radius:

  1. In the tools bar, click on the Turning Radius Tool icon . By default, the turnings with a radius below 3.20m are displayed in orange. You can modify the default radius according to your needs.
  2. (optional) In the Turning Radius Tool section of the left pane, enter the desired radius in the Radius field.

docs.title: Identifying a region of interest
docs.text: The Region of interest tool allows you to define specific regions and identify the similar regions by color. The types of region of interest for the vehicle are defined by the software engineering teams. They define the types of region of interest according to their needs.

docs.title: Creating a region of interest
docs.text:
To create a region of interest:

  1. In the tools bar, click on the Region of interest icon .

    Result: A small square hovers with the pointer in the map window. The square represents one point of the region of interest.

  2. Click to place the points of the region of interest.

After you have created a region of interest, you can identify similar regions by color. For more information, see Identifying similar regions of interest.

docs.title: Identifying similar regions of interest
docs.text:
To define similar regions of interest, you need to use the same name prefix. The regions of interest with the same name prefix are in the same color.

To identify similar regions of interest:

  1. In the tool bar, click on the HDMap Selection icon .
  2. Select the region of interest you have created.
  3. In the Region of Interest section at the bottom of the left pane,
  4. In the Description field, enter a name with the following naming convention: prefix_name. The regions of interest are sorted by the prefix.

Example

you want to create regions of interest to identify some buildings. The names of the regions of interest could be "building_high", "building_medium" and "building_small". All the regions of interest with the prefix "building" are sorted in the same category and colored in the same color.

In the Elements left pane, you can view or hide the regions of interest you have created.

docs.title: Selecting elements
docs.text: HDmap selection is an essential tool for the creation of maps. With HDmap selection, you can select, edit, move and delete elements.

docs.title: Selecting elements
docs.text:
To select an element:

  1. In the tool bar, click on the HDMap Selection icon .
  2. Do one of the following:
    • Click on the element you want to select.
    • Click and drag the mouse cursor to select the elements.

Result: The selected elements are colored in yellow. At the bottom of the left pane, you can see the properties and the number of selected elements.

docs.title: Editing selected elements
docs.text:
To edit an element:

  1. In the tool bar, click on the HDMap Selection icon .

  2. Select the element you want to edit.

    Result: The selected element appears in yellow and there are control points at each end of the selected element.

  3. Click on a control point to edit the element according to your needs.

docs.title: Moving selected elements
docs.text:
To move an element:

  1. In the tool bar, click on the HDMap Selection icon
  2. Click on the element you want to move and place it at the selected position.

docs.title: Deleting selected elements
docs.text:
To delete an element:

  1. In the tool bar, click on the HDMap Selection icon .
  2. Click on the element you want to delete.
  3. Right-click and select Delete.

docs.title: Creating traffic signs
docs.text:
You can place the traffic signs at their actual position in the site. You can also define the behaviors and the priorities at a traffic sign.

Tip

Since traffic signs are part of the HD Maps behaviors, it is highly recommended to read the following part: HD Maps Behaviors before you start creating traffic signs. After reading this part, you will be able to better understand how HD Maps behaviors work and how to define them according to your needs.

docs.title: About Stop signs
docs.text:
The stop sign is defined by the following features:

  • the position of the sign
  • 0 to N stops lanes which correspond to the N stop points where the vehicle should stop.
  • 1 to M concerned itineraries with their associated priority areas

A stop sign can have several concerned itineraries. The concerned itinerary corresponds to the mission and defines the priority areas that need to be considered (see Figure A). You can also create a stop sign without an associated concerned itinerary. In this case, the stop sign is always considered.

Figure A: A stop sign with a perpendicular priority lane

Note

The Yield sign edition is similar to the Stop sign. They have the same properties.

docs.title: Creating a stop sign
docs.text:
When you create a stop sign, you only create the physical sign and the associated road marking. If you want the vehicle to stop at the stop sign, you need to define the behaviors and priorities.

To create a stop sign:

  1. In the tools bar, click on the Stop sign icon .

    Result: In 2D mode, a cross hovers with the pointer in the map window. The cross represents the stop sign.

  2. Click at the position where you want to place the stop sign.

    Result: In 2D mode, a square hovers with the pointer in the map window. The square represents one end of the stop road marking.

  3. Click to place each end of the stop road marking.

docs.title: Defining behaviors and priorities
docs.text:
The vehicle stops when the front end of the vehicle is at a specific distance from the end of the stop lane. This distance is defined in the configuration file decision.conf. The parameter planner/stop_distance allows you to define the distance..

To define behaviors and priorities:

  1. Select the stop sign you have created.

  2. In the Stop Sign section of left pane, click on the + icon next to the empty Stop Lanes field.

    Result: A white line hovers with the pointer on edges. The white line represents the stop line: the position where the vehicle stops.

  3. Click to place the stop line.

    Result: The lane on which you placed the stop line is identified in the Stop Lanes section of the left pane.

  4. Click on the icons - or + to define the Itinerary Depth. If you define the Itinerary Depth at 1, the current itinerary will take into account the following edge as part of its itinerary. If you define the Itinerary Depth at 2, the current itinerary will take into account the two following edges as part of its itinerary and so on.

  5. (optional) If there is more than one possible itinerary at the stop line, select a path in the Itineraries drop-down list.

    Depending on the selected itinerary, you can define a priority area. In other words, you can define that an edge is a priority over another edge.

  6. (optional) To define a priority area, click on the + icon next to the empty Priority Areas field then select the priority edge for this itinerary.

    Result: The selected priority edge is colored in orange. And the selected priority edges are identified in the Priority Areas section of the left pane.

docs.title: Deleting stop lanes and priority areas
docs.text:
To delete a stop lane:

  1. Select the stop sign you have created.
  2. In the Stop Sign section of left pane, select the stop lane you want to delete.
  3. Click on the x icon next to the Stop Lanes field.

You have deleted the stop lane. To delete a priority area, follow the same procedure in the Priority Areas field.

docs.title: Yield sign
docs.text: The yield sign edition is similar to the Stop sign. They have the same properties. For more information on yield signs, see About stop signs.

docs.title: Creating a yield sign
docs.text:
To create a yield sign:

  1. In the tools bar, click on the Yield sign icon .

    Result: In 2D mode, a cross hovers with the pointer in the map window. The cross represents the yield sign.

  2. Click at the position where you want to place the yield sign.

    Result: In 2D mode, a square hovers with the pointer in the map window. The square represents one end of the yield road marking.

  3. Click to place each end of the yield road marking.

docs.title: Defining behaviors and priorities
docs.text:
The vehicle stops when the front end of the vehicle is on the yield sign position.

To define behaviors and priorities:

  1. Select the stop sign you have created.

  2. In the Yield Sign section of left pane, click on the + icon next to the empty Stop Lanes field.

    Result: A white line hovers with the pointer on edges. The white line represents the stop line: the position where the vehicle stops.

  3. Click to place the stop line.

    Result: The lane on which you placed the stop line is identified in the Stop Lanes section of the left pane.

  4. Click on the icons - or + to define the Itinerary Depth. If you define the Itinerary Depth at 1, the current itinerary will take into account the following edge as part of its itinerary. If you define the Itinerary Depth at 2, the current itinerary will take into account the two following edges as part of its itinerary and so on.

  5. (optional) If there is more than one possible itinerary at the stop line, select a path in the Itineraries drop-down list.

    Depending on the selected itinerary, you can define a priority area. In other words, you can define that an edge is a priority over another edge.

  6. (optional) To define a priority area, click on the + icon next to the empty Priority Areas field then select the priority edge for this itinerary.

    Result: The selected priority edge is colored in orange. And the selected priority edges are identified in the Priority Areas section of the left pane.

docs.title: Deleting stop lanes and priority areas
docs.text:
To delete a stop lane:

  1. Select the stop sign you have created.
  2. In the Stop Sign section of left pane, select the stop lane you want to delete.
  3. Click on the x icon next to the Stop Lanes field.

You have deleted the stop lane. To delete a priority area, follow the same procedure in the Priority Areas field.

docs.title: About traffic lights
docs.text:
Traffic lights are defined by the following features:

  • the position of the traffic light in the map
  • 0 to N stop lanes which correspond to the N stop points where the vehicle should stop for the traffic light. You can create several affected lanes for one traffic light.
  • 1 to M concerned itineraries with their associated priority areas

A stop sign can have several concerned itineraries. The concerned itinerary corresponds to the mission and defines the priority areas that need to be considered (see Figures B and C).

Note

As of Mar 10th, 2020, the assigned priorities are not yet considered for traffic lights.

Concerned itinerary with one associated priority lane

Concerned itinerary with two associated priority lanes

docs.title: Creating a traffic light
docs.text:
To create a traffic light:

  1. In the tools bar, click on the Traffic Light icon .

    Result: In 2D mode, a cross hovers with the pointer in the map window. The cross represents the traffic light.

  2. Click at the position where you want to place the traffic light.

    Result: In 2D mode, square hovers with the pointer in the map window. The square represents one end of the traffic light road marking.

  3. Click to place each end of the traffic light road marking.

docs.title: Defining behaviors and priorities
docs.text:
The vehicle stops when the front end of the vehicle is at a specific distance from the end of the stop lane. This distance is defined in the configuration file decision.conf. The parameter planner/stop_distance allows you to define the distance.

To define behaviors and priorities:

  1. Select the stop sign you have created.

  2. In the Traffic Light section of left pane, click on the + icon next to the empty Stop Lanes field.

    Result: A white line hovers with the pointer on edges. The white line represents the stop line: the position where the vehicle stops.

  3. Click to place the stop line.

    Result: The lane on which you placed the stop line is identified in the Stop Lanes section of the left pane.

  4. Click on the icons - or + to define the Itinerary Depth. If you define the Itinerary Depth at 1, the current itinerary will take into account the following edge as part of its itinerary. If you define the Itinerary Depth at 2, the current itinerary will take into account the two following edges as part of its itinerary and so on.

  5. (optional) If there is more than one possible itinerary at the stop line, select a path in the Itineraries drop-down list.

    Depending on the selected itinerary, you can define a priority area. In other words, you can define that an edge is a priority over another edge.

  6. (optional) To define a priority area, click on the + icon next to the empty Priority Areas field then select the priority edge for this itinerary.

    Result: The selected priority edge is colored in orange. And the selected priority edges are identified in the Priority Areas section of the left pane.

docs.title: Deleting stop lanes and priority areas
docs.text:
To delete a stop lane:

  1. Select the stop sign you have created.
  2. In the Stop Sign section of left pane, select the stop lane you want to delete.
  3. Click on the x icon next to the Stop Lanes field.

You have deleted the stop lane. To delete a priority area, follow the same procedure in the Priority Areas field.

docs.title: Defining the V2X settings
docs.text:
To define the V2X settings:

  1. In the Traffic Light section of the left pane, check the V2X box.

    Result: The V2X settings appears.

  2. In the V2X drop down list, select the appropriate V2X standard.

  3. Enter the following parameters:

    • Region ID
    • Intersection ID
    • Traffic light ID

docs.title: Creating a virtual sign
docs.text:
You can use virtual signs to place traffic signs that are not actually on the site. For example, it can be a priority on the right where there is no physical sign. You can create the following virtual traffic signs:

  • Stop sign
  • Yield sign
  • Traffic light

To create a virtual sign:

  1. In the tools bar, click on the icon of one of the following traffic signs: Stop, Yield and Traffic light.

  2. In the Sign Creator section at the bottom of the left pane, check the box Virtual.

    Note

    You can only place virtual signs on edges.

  3. Click at the position where you want to place the virtual sign. The vehicle stops at the position of the virtual sign.

  4. Define behaviors and priorities of the virtual sign. For more information on how to define behaviors and priorities, see the relevant section: Defining behaviors and priorities.

docs.title: Defining a desired speed
docs.text:
You can define a desired speed on a selected path or an itinerary.

Tip

Since Desired speed is part of the HD Maps behaviors, it is highly recommended to read the following part: HD Maps Behaviors before you start defining speed on a path or an itinerary. After reading this part, you will be able to better understand how HD Maps behaviors work and how to define them according to your needs.

docs.title: About desired speeds
docs.text:
There are two types of velocity limits:

  • Default desired speed: The default desired speed for a lane. The default desired speed applies on both directions of the lane.

    Note

    It is highly recommended to use the Default desired speed property to define the vehicle speed on a path. The Desired speed behavior allows you to modify the default desired speed on a specific part of the path. You can define the default desired speed in the properties of edges. For more information, see Creating edges.

  • Desired speed: a speed defined on a lane portion which takes over the default desired speed on this portion. A desired speed is defined by the following features:

    • A direction
    • A start and an end position on one or several consecutive lanes
    • An optional concerned itinerary

If you don't define a concerned itinerary, the speed limit is automatically applied to the lanes on which a direction is defined.

docs.title: Define the vehicle speed on a path or an itinerary
docs.text:
The velocity limit is considered when the front end of the vehicle is between the start and the end of the defined zone.

To define the vehicle speed on a path or an itinerary:

  1. In the tool bar, click on the Desired speed icon .

  2. In the Desired Speed Creator section of the left pane, enter the desired vehicle speed in the Speed Value field.

    Result: A line hovers with the pointer on edges.

    Desired speed with a right direction

  3. Click to place the start of the desired speed.

    Result: A pink line appears at the position where you placed the start of the desired speed. A second pink line hovers with the pointer on edges. It represents the moment when the desired speed is no longer applied. You can also add an itinerary and select the path in which you want to place the itinerary end.

  4. (optional) To add an itinerary, check the Add itinerary box in the Desired Speed Creator section of the left pane.

  5. (optional) To select a path at an intersection, select a path in the Itineraries drop-down list in the Desired Speed Creator section of the left pane.

  6. Click to place the end of the desired speed.

    Result: The defined vehicle speed is applied between the vehicle speed tag. The vehicle speed tag is represented by a square and and an arrow. The speed is indicated in the square.

    Desired speed with a concerned itinerary defined

docs.title: Editing the itinerary start
docs.text:
Before you edit an itinerary start, make sure you have added an itinerary when you have defined the vehicle speed. For more information on adding an itinerary, see Define the vehicle speed on a path or an itinerary .

To edit the itinerary start:

  1. In the tool bar, click on the HDMap Selection icon .

  2. Select the desired speed.

  3. In the Desired Speed section of the left pane, click on + Advanced tools

    Result: The path where you have defined the vehicle speed is colored in purple and the itinerary line is blue.

  4. Click on the Edit itinerary start button.

    Result: A line hovers with the pointer on the path.

  5. Click to place the itinerary start.

docs.title: Editing the itinerary
docs.text:
To edit the itinerary:

  1. In the tool bar, click on the HDMap Selection icon .

  2. Select the desired speed.

  3. Click on the Edit itinerary button.

  4. Click on the icons - or + to define the Itinerary Depth. By default, the itinerary depth is defined at 0. If you define the Itinerary Depth at 1, the current itinerary will take into account the following edge as part of its itinerary. If you define the Itinerary Depth at 2, the current itinerary will take into account the two following edges as part of its itinerary and so on.

  5. (optional) In the Itinerary field, select a path in the drop-down list if available.

    Result: The itinerary follows the path you have selected. The itinerary is represented by a blue line.

  6. Click on the Apply button.

docs.title: Creating a terminal
docs.text: The terminal tool allows you to create and place a terminal sign at a specific position. Before you create a terminal, make sure you have created edges. You can only place terminals on edges.

docs.title: Creating a terminal
docs.text:
To create a terminal:

  1. In the tool bar, click on the Terminal icon .
  2. Place the terminal at the position you want.
  3. (optional) In the Elements left pane, rename the terminal in the Terminal section.

In the Terminal section at the bottom of the left pane, you can view the following information: terminal name, terminal ID and the terminal position (x,y,z).

docs.title: Defining turn signals
docs.text:
You can define at which point in the itinerary the vehicle activates and deactivates the selected turn signal.

Tip

Since turn signals are part of the HD Maps behaviors, it is highly recommended to read the following part: HD Maps Behaviors before you start defining turn signals. After reading this part, you will be able to better understand how HD Maps behaviors work and how to define them according to your needs.

docs.title: About turn signals
docs.text:
A turn signal is defined by the following features:

  • a direction
  • a start and an end position. It should start long enough before the turn and end at the end of the turn.
  • a concerned itinerary which starts in the zone of the turn signal and ends on or after the end of the turn signal.

docs.title: Concerned itinerary
docs.text:
The concerned itinerary should start just before the turn (see Figure A). If the mission stops before the turn, the itinerary won't include the turn signal and the vehicle won't blink unnecessarily.

Figure A: The concerned itinerary starts when the turn starts.

The concerned itinerary should end when the turn is over. It should not overlap with the lane following the turn. Otherwise, the vehicle blinks in the following straight lane (see Figure B).

Figure B: Left: The behavior starts too early and is included in the mission when it should not be. Right: The behavior ends too late and the vehicle blinks pointlessly.

docs.title: Defining a turn signal in a selected itinerary
docs.text:
The selected turn signal is activated when the front end of the vehicle is between the start and the end of the defined zone.

To define a turn signal in a selected itinerary:

  1. In the tools bar, click on the Turn Signal icon .

    Result: A line hovers with the pointer on edges. The line represents the itinerary start which is the moment when the turn signal is activated.

  2. Click to place the itinerary start.

    Result: An orange line and arrow appear at the position where you placed the itinerary start. A second orange line and arrow hover with the pointer on edges. It represents the end of the itinerary which is the moment when the turn signal is deactivated. At an intersection of two paths or more, select the path in which you want to place the itinerary end.

  3. (optional) To select a path at an intersection, select a path in the Itineraries drop-down list in the Turn Signal Creator section of the left pane.

  4. Click to place the itinerary end.

  5. In the Turn Signal section of the left pane, select the left or right arrow to activate the left or right turn signal.

Result: The selected turn signal is activated between the two orange arrows.

docs.title: Editing the itinerary start
docs.text:
To edit the itinerary start:

  1. In the tool bar, click on the HDMap Selection icon .

  2. Select the turn signal.

  3. In the Turn Signal section of the left pane, click on + Advanced tools

  4. Click on the Edit itinerary start button.

    Result: A line hovers with the pointer on edges. The line represents the itinerary start which is the moment when the turn signal is activated.

    Note

    You can only place the itinerary start between the start and the end of the behavior.

  5. Click to place the itinerary start.

docs.title: Editing itineraries
docs.text:
To edit the itinerary:

  1. In the tool bar, click on the HDMap Selection icon .

  2. Select the turn signal.

  3. Click on the Edit itinerary button.

  4. Click on the icons - or + to define the Itinerary Depth. By default, the itinerary depth is defined at 0. If you define the Itinerary Depth at 1, the current itinerary will take into account the following edge as part of its itinerary. If you define the Itinerary Depth at 2, the current itinerary will take into account the two following edges as part of its itinerary and so on.

  5. (optional) In the Itinerary field, select a path in the drop-down list if available.

    Result: The itinerary follows the path you have selected. The itinerary is represented by a blue line.

docs.title: Testing the size of a vehicle
docs.text: The Volume test tool allows you to define the length, width and height of a vehicle and test this vehicle on a lane.

docs.title: Testing a vehicle on a path
docs.text:
To test a vehicle on a path:

  1. In the tools bar, click on the Volume test icon .

    Note

    You can only test a vehicle on a lane.

  2. In the Volume test section at the bottom of the Elements left pane, enter the following parameters:

    • Length (in meters)
    • Width (in meters)
    • Height (in meters)

  3. Hover the vehicle on the lane to test the dimensions.

docs.title: Saving LiDAR maps
docs.text: After you have edited LiDAR maps, you can save and export LiDAR maps according to your needs.

docs.title: Saving LiDAR maps
docs.text:
To save a LiDAR map:

  1. In the top bar, click File > Save As.

    Result: A Save as... window appears.

  2. Select the location where you want to save the map.

  3. Click Save.

    Result: You have saved the LiDAR map and the filename extension of LiDAR maps is .dat.

docs.title: Exporting LiDAR maps
docs.text:
To export a LiDAR map:

  1. In the top bar, click File > Export.

    Result: A Map Editor window appears (see Figure A).

    Figure A: Map Editor export window

  2. Depending of the type of export you want, select one of the following:

    • 2D Map: the points are flatten, and you can define the height range of the points you want to export: z min and z max (see Figure A).
    • Intensity: you can define the height range (z min and z max) and the intensity threshold (intensity min) of the points you want to export.
    • LogPoints: you can export all the logpoints of the map. Logpoints are the scan centers.

  3. Click on the Export button.

    Result: A Save as... window appears.

  4. Select the location where you want to export the map.

  5. Click Save.

    Result: You have exported the LiDAR map. If you have exported the map as 2D Map or Intensity map, the filename extension is .dat. If you have exported the map as LogPoints, the filename extension is .m.

docs.title: Selecting clusters
docs.text: You can select already identified clusters and classify them into categories. Clusters are groups of points identified by algorithms.

docs.title: Selecting clusters
docs.text:
To select clusters:

  1. In the tool bar, click on the Cluster Selection icon .

  2. To select a cluster, click on a cluster in the map.

    Result: The following cluster information appears in the Cluster Selection section at the bottom of the left pane (see Figure A):

    • ID
    • Classification
    • Points

    Figure A: Selected cluster information

docs.title: Classifying clusters
docs.text:
To classify a cluster:

  1. In the tool bar, click on the Cluster Selection icon .

  2. Click on a cluster in the map.

  3. Right click on the cluster.

    Result: A context menu appears (see Figure B).

  4. Select Classify > The classification of the selected cluster .

    Figure B: Classifying a cluster as building

docs.title: Selecting clusters with the same classification
docs.text:
To select clusters with the same classification:

  1. In the tool bar, click on the Cluster Selection icon .

  2. Click on a cluster in the map.

  3. Right click on the cluster.

    Result: A context menu appears.

  4. Select Select Same.

    Result: All the clusters with the same classification appear in color in the map. Depending on the mode set in the color switch , the clusters will either appear in the same color or in random colors. For more information on colorization, see the following section on colorization.

docs.title: Selecting cuboids
docs.text: You can manually identify groups of points as clusters and classify the identified clusters.

docs.title: Defining a cluster
docs.text:
To define a cluster:

  1. In the tool bar, click on the Cuboid Selection icon .

  2. Hold the left mouse button on the cluster you want to define.

    Result: A cube with a blue top side, a right green side, and a red front side appears.

  3. Drag the mouse to roughly select the cluster.

    Result: The cluster is contained in the cube. A pane with the top, right, and front views of the cluster in 2D appears on the right (see Figure A).

    Figure A: The identified cluster and the three views of the cluster on the right.

  4. To better adjust the selection, use the corner handles of the three views in 2D.

  5. Right click on the selected cluster in the map.

    Result: A context menu appears.

  6. Select Classify > The classification of the selected cluster .

docs.title: Exporting cluster coordinates
docs.text:
To export cluster coordinates:

  1. In the tool bar, click on the Cuboid Selection icon .

  2. In the Cuboid selection section in the left pane, check Export geometry (see Figure B).

    Figure B: Export geometry in the left pane

  3. Select and define the cluster from which you want to export the coordinates. For more information on how to select and define clusters, see Defining a cluster.

    Result: A file with the cluster coordinates is automatically created in the same location as the lidar map. The file extension is .labelcubes.

docs.title: Selecting points
docs.text: You can view information about points and leverage this information according to your needs.

docs.title: Viewing point information
docs.text:
To view point information

  1. In the tool bar, click on the Point Selection icon .

  2. To select a point, click on a point in the map.

    Result: The following point information appears in the Point Selection section at the bottom of the left pane (see Figure A):

    • ID
    • Coordinates in X, Y, Z
    • Intensity
    • Label

    Figure A: Selected point information

docs.title: Comparing two points
docs.text:
To compare two points:

  1. In the tool bar, click on the Point Selection icon .

  2. Press and hold the Ctrl key and click on the two points you want to compare.

    Result: The selected points are colored in different colors. By default, the first selected point is in yellow, and the second one in orange. You can view and compare the information of the two points in the Point Selection section at the bottom of the left pane (see Figure B). Point information takes the color of the point selected.

    Figure B: Information from the two selected points in the respective color of their points

docs.title: Exporting a list of point coordinates
docs.text:
To export a list of point coordinates:

  1. In the tool bar, click on the Point Selection icon .

  2. To select a point, click on a point in the map.

  3. In the Picking field in the Point Selection section at the bottom of the left pane, click on the + (see Figure C).

    Result: The point coordinates appear in the Picking field.

    Figure C: Point coordinates in the Picking field.

  4. To save the point coordinates as a file, click on the download icon .

    Result: A Save As... window appears.

  5. Select the location where you want to save the file and enter a name for the file then click Save.

    Result: You have created a .path file with all the selected point coordinates.

docs.title: Selecting scans
docs.text: You can select one or multiple scans and view information related to the selected scans.

docs.title: Viewing scan information
docs.text:
To view scan information:

  1. In the map window, click on the Show scans centers icon .

    Result: The scan centers appear on the map.

  2. In the tool bar, click on the Scan Selection icon .

  3. To select a scan, click on a scan center.

    Result: Information related to the selected scan appears in the Scan Selection section at the bottom of the left pane (see Figure A).

    Figure A: Selected scan information

docs.title: Comparing two scans
docs.text:
To compare two scans:

  1. In the map window, click on the Show scans centers icon .

    Result: The scan centers appear on the map.

  2. In the tool bar, click on the Scan Selection icon .

  3. Press and hold the Ctrl key and click on the scan centers of the two scans you want to compare.

    Result: The selected scan centers are colored in different colors. By default, the first selected scan center is in yellow, and the second one in orange. You can view and compare the information of the two scans in the Scan Selection section at the bottom of the left pane (see Figure B). Scan information takes the color of the scan center selected.

    Figure B: Information from the two selected scans in the respective color of their scan centers

docs.title: Selecting multiple scans
docs.text:
To select multiple scans:

  1. In the map window, click on the Show scans centers icon .

    Result: The scan centers appear on the map.

  2. In the tool bar, click on the Scan Selection icon .

  3. Do one of the following:

    • Press and hold the Shift key and click on the first and the last scan center of the set of scans you want to select.
    • Click and hold the left mouse button and move the cursor to select a set of scans.

    Result: The set of selected scan centers are colored in the same color. You can view the number of scans you have selected in the Scan Selection section at the bottom of the left pane (see Figure C).
